confidence.title: Data Confidence & Coverage Transparency
confidence.tracked_high: Tracked zone with direct rover or orbiter instrumentation. Physical parameters come from curated NASA mission datasets.
confidence.tracked_mars_curated: Curated Mars mission zone: surface weather and dust come from Curiosity REMS / Perseverance MEDA telemetry, solar flux from orbital geometry, and terrain/ice constants from published MRO/LOLA references.
confidence.tracked_moon_curated: Curated Moon zone: observation timestamps come from NASA PDS ODE LRO Diviner, diurnal temperatures from Stefan-Boltzmann radiative physics, and terrain/ice constants from published LRO references.
confidence.mars_extrapolated: Honest estimation notice: This coordinate is {{km}} km from {{site}}. Atmospheric telemetry is extrapolated from Curiosity REMS (Gale Crater) + orbital solar geometry, while terrain (slope, roughness, albedo, ice) is estimated by Martian latitude regime.
confidence.moon_pds_partial: Partial orbital coverage: {{count}} real LRO Diviner products were found in NASA PDS ODE for this region, combined with radiative thermal physics. Slope, roughness, and ice are estimated by lunar regime.
confidence.moon_estimated: Honest estimation notice: No direct LRO Diviner products were found in NASA PDS ODE for this exact cell. Surface and terrain parameters are estimated from lunar latitude/longitude regime and Stefan-Boltzmann radiative physics.

learn.title: Planetary Physics Lab — What if…?
learn.subtitle: Local SI-unit simulators connected to your selected body and site. Compare Earth, Mars, and the Moon with explicit equations and limits.
learn.noComparisonHint: Select an Earth H3 cell in Compare to link real terrestrial slope measurements to these challenges.

weight.question: Does your mass change if you travel to Mars or the Moon?
weight.intro: Mass (kg) is invariant; what changes is gravitational force or weight (N).
weight.limits: Assumptions: standard mean surface gravity (Earth 9.80665; Mars 3.71; Moon 1.62 m/s²). A spring scale calibrated on Earth would read lower kgf, not lower mass.

jump.question: How high would you jump with the same takeoff speed?
jump.intro: At equal takeoff velocity, peak height scales inversely with g.
jump.limits: Ideal vertical model without air drag or pressurized spacesuit load. On Mars (~2.64×) and the Moon (~6.05×), suit mass and biomechanics limit real impulse.

projectile.question: How does a projectile parabola change across worlds?
projectile.intro: Ideal ballistic trajectory without aerodynamic drag from the same launch height.
projectile.svgLabel: Comparison of parabolic trajectories on Earth, Mars, and Moon
projectile.limits: No atmospheric drag; ideal max range occurs at 45° and does not depend on mass in this model. On Earth, air slows light projectiles.

waves.question: What happens to waves in a pool inside a pressurized habitat?
waves.intro: Simulated inside a pressurized, thermally controlled habitat (not outdoors on Mars).
waves.limits: Valid only in the shallow-water regime (depth d ≪ wavelength λ): on Mars wave speed is ~0.615× (~38.5% slower). Deep-water waves depend on λ.

rocks.question: Is it equally easy to accelerate a rock even if it weighs less?
rocks.intro: Lifting against gravity takes less force, but horizontal acceleration requires the exact same net force F = m·a.
rocks.limits: Inertia (mass) does not decrease on Mars or the Moon. Lower weight also reduces maximum static friction with the ground.

rover.question: How does gravity affect a rover climbing a slope?
rover.intro: Inclined-plane force decomposition linked to the slopes of the active site and Earth analog.
rover.limits: Ideal rigid model (tan θ ≤ μ). In real Martian/lunar regolith or loose Atacama sand, wheel sinkage and soil cohesion reduce traction before the ideal limit.
rover.diagramLabel: Interactive free-body force diagram for rover on a {{slope}}-degree slope

wind.question: Does a 100 km/h wind on Mars push as hard as on Earth?
wind.intro: Dynamic pressure scales with air density ρ: Mars atmosphere is ~60× less dense than Earth.
wind.limits: Illustrative mean surface densities (Earth ~1.225 kg/m³; Mars ~0.020 kg/m³). Real density varies with elevation, temperature, and season.

water.question: What happens to open-air liquid water in Antofagasta vs Mars?
water.intro: Liquid water stability depends on both pressure and temperature; Martian pressure (~0.61 kPa) sits right near the triple point.
water.limits: Educational approximation using water triple point (0.611657 kPa; 0.01 °C) and Clausius-Clapeyron relation. Brines (Atacama salts or Martian perchlorates) shift freezing points.

curiosities.pressureTitle: Liquid water outdoors on Mars (~0.6 kPa)
curiosities.pressureDesc: Unlike Antofagasta (~101 kPa at sea level), Martian surface pressure is ~0.6 kPa: exposed liquid water boils, freezes, or sublimates depending on temperature.
curiosities.dustDesc: Even with fast winds, Mars thin atmosphere (~1% of Earth density) produces lower dynamic pressure q = 0.5·ρ·v² at the same wind speed.
curiosities.atacamaTitle: Why is Atacama / Yungay a key analog?
curiosities.atacamaDesc: Extreme hyperaridity, UV flux, and saline soils allow studying Mars-analog processes, while gravity (1 g), pressure, and cosmic radiation remain irreproducible.
curiosities.soundTitle: Sound on Mars (~240 m/s and attenuated)
curiosities.soundDesc: In Mars thin CO₂ atmosphere (~0.6 kPa), sound travels around 240 m/s (vs ~343 m/s on Earth) and high frequencies attenuate rapidly. Speaking outdoors without a suit is unsafe.
curiosities.solTitle: A Martian sol lasts 24 h 39 min (vs 29.5 days on the Moon)
curiosities.solDesc: A Martian sol is just 39 minutes longer than an Earth day, whereas the lunar day/night cycle lasts ~29.5 Earth days, challenging solar power storage.
curiosities.commsTitle: Earth–Mars signal delay (3 to 22 min one-way)
curiosities.commsDesc: Depending on orbital distance (55 to 401 million km), radio signals take ~3 to ~22 minutes each way—requiring local autonomous rover navigation.

mass.question: 1. If a 70 kg student travels to Jezero Crater, what happens to their mass and weight?
mass.optA: Mass drops to ~26 kg and weight stays 686 N
mass.optB: Mass stays 70 kg and weight drops to ~260 N
mass.optC: Both mass and weight drop to one-third
mass.explanation: Mass is intrinsic (70 kg). Weight is gravitational force P = m·g ≈ 70 × 3.71 ≈ 259.7 N.

roverDynamic.question: 2. At the active slope ({{slope}}°) near {{site}}, what happens to a 100 kg rover compared to Earth?
roverDynamic.optA: It climbs with higher traction because it weighs less
roverDynamic.optB: Parallel force drops (from {{earthN}} N to {{marsN}} N), but normal force also drops (to {{marsNormalN}} N on Mars)
roverDynamic.optC: A 15° slope is universally safe on any terrain
roverDynamic.explanation: Lower gravity reduces parallel force ({{earthN}} N → {{marsN}} N), but also lowers normal force ({{marsNormalN}} N) and max friction μ·N.

nonReplicable.question: 3. Which Mars variable CANNOT be replicated in open-air field trials in Antofagasta?
nonReplicable.optB: Surface UV irradiance and low relative humidity
nonReplicable.optC: Gravity (0.38 g), ~0.6 kPa CO₂ atmosphere, and ionizing GCR radiation
nonReplicable.explanation: Irreproducible breakage boundaries B (gravity, atmospheric pressure, cosmic radiation) cannot be replicated in open Earth field trials.

distributions.question: 4. What does it mean when two slope distributions are similar between Jezero and Atacama?
distributions.optA: Both sites are identical for landing without further tests
distributions.optB: Partial morphological similarity in an independent variable X, not full physical equivalence
distributions.explanation: Ckepi decouples X, Y, and B: geometric slope similarity never implies complete environmental or mechanical equivalence.

sound.q: Why would your voice sound different and much quieter on Mars?
sound.a: In Mars thin CO₂ atmosphere (~0.6 kPa), sound travels at ~240 m/s (vs ~343 m/s on Earth) and high frequencies attenuate quickly.

sol.q: How long is a day on Mars?
sol.a: One Martian sol lasts 24 h 39 min 35 s—almost identical to an Earth day, which helps teams schedule rover operations.

comms.q: Can you drive a Mars rover with a live joystick from Earth?
comms.a: No: depending on orbital distance, radio signals take ~3 to ~22 minutes one-way, so rovers rely on onboard autonomous navigation.

radiation.q: How much radiation does an astronaut face on Mars?
radiation.a: Without a global magnetic field or thick atmosphere, surface radiation far exceeds Earths ~2.4 mSv/yr average.

olympus.q: How tall is Olympus Mons compared to Atacama volcanoes?
olympus.a: It rises ~21.9 km high (~3× Everest) and spans ~600 km wide, yet its average slope is surprisingly gentle (~5°).

temperature.q: How much can temperature swing in a single Martian day?
temperature.a: In craters like Jezero or Gale, diurnal temperature swings exceed 60–80 K due to low thermal inertia and thin air.

blueSunset.q: What color are sunsets on Mars?
blueSunset.a: Bluish near the Sun: fine Martian dust scatters red light at wide angles while letting blue light pass forward.

phobos.q: Which way does Phobos rise and set in the Martian sky?
phobos.a: Phobos orbits faster than Mars rotates (~7 h 39 min), so it rises in the west and sets in the east.

dustStorm.q: Can dust storms cover the entire planet Mars?
dustStorm.a: Yes: planet-encircling storms can dim sunlight for weeks, even though wind dynamic pressure remains low due to thin air.

moonTemp.q: What extreme temperatures does a lunar rover face?
moonTemp.a: With no atmosphere, the surface swings from ~390 K (+117 °C) in sunlight to ~100 K (-173 °C) during lunar night.

moonFootprints.q: Why are Apollo footprints still intact after more than 50 years?
moonFootprints.a: The Moon has no wind or rain; only gradual micrometeorite impacts erode regolith over millions of years.

moonDay.q: How long is a full solar day on the Moon?
moonDay.a: About 29.5 Earth days (~14 days of sunlight followed by ~14 days of darkness), requiring robust energy storage.

atacamaRovers.q: Why has NASA tested rover prototypes in the Atacama Desert?
atacamaRovers.a: Because of extreme hyperaridity, saline soils, high UV flux, and near-zero vegetation in sectors like Yungay.

perchlorate.q: Which chemical compound do Atacama and Mars soils share?
perchlorate.a: Both contain natural perchlorates and salts, valuable for studying regolith chemistry and extremophile limits.

distribution.noteRadBody: On Mars, Curiosity/RAD measured ~0.64 mSv/day (~230 mSv/yr GCR+SEP; Hassler et al., 2014, Science). Atacama (~2.4 mSv/yr) validates UV optics and terrain, not nuclear GCR shielding.
distribution.noteBioBody: This comparison quantifies geomorphological and thermo-radiative fidelity for rover traction, LiDAR navigation, and ISRU drills; it does not claim surface biological habitability.

threeWorlds.title: Three Worlds in Your Hand: Earth · Moon · Mars (STEAM Literacy)
threeWorlds.subtitle: Explore with verified NASA NSSDCA facts what changes across worlds and why Antofagasta trains real space missions.
threeWorlds.speechScript: Welcome to Ckepi, Three Worlds in Your Hand. If a backpack weighs 10 kilograms in Antofagasta, on the Moon it weighs only 1.7 kilograms and on Mars 3.8 kilograms. Today we compare {{earthSite}} with {{targetSite}}: the statistical slope difference at 30 meters scale is {{w1Slope}} degrees. In Antofagasta we can field-test rover wheels, LiDAR cameras, and drills, while reduced gravity, thin air, and cosmic radiation require specialized simulation chambers.

earth.name: Earth (Antofagasta)
earth.summary: Our hyper-arid natural laboratory protected by a dense atmosphere and global magnetosphere.
earth.backpack: A 10 kg backpack feels like 10.0 kg (1.00 g).
earth.air: Breathable air at 1013 mbar (N₂/O₂); supports standard drones and convective cooling.
earth.dayAndTemp: Solar day: 24 h 00 min · Global mean temp.: ~15 °C (288 K).
earth.radiation: Natural background radiation: ~2.4 mSv/yr (shielded by magnetosphere and atmosphere).

moon.name: Moon (South Pole / Maria)
moon.summary: Airless world with permanently shadowed polar craters and electrostatically charged dust.
moon.backpack: A 10 kg backpack feels like 1.7 kg (0.166 g).
moon.air: Hard vacuum (0 mbar): no sound, no wind, and no aerodynamic parachutes.
moon.dayAndTemp: Solar day: ~29.5 Earth days · Extreme thermal swings (>260 K).
moon.radiation: Unshielded surface radiation: ~380 mSv/yr without magnetosphere.

mars.name: Mars (Jezero / Gale Crater)
mars.summary: Cold desert world with a thin CO₂ atmosphere, ancient lake deltas, and active dust storms.
mars.backpack: A 10 kg backpack feels like 3.8 kg (0.38 g).
mars.air: Thin CO₂ atmosphere (~6.1 mbar, <1% of Earth): requires high-RPM rotorcraft.
mars.dayAndTemp: Solar day (Sol): 24 h 39 min · Mean surface temp.: −63 °C (210 K).
mars.radiation: Surface radiation measured by Curiosity/RAD: ~230 mSv/yr (~0.64 mSv/day, Hassler et al. 2014).

quiz.question: STEAM micro-challenge: you must test a rover's suspension for the floor of Jezero Crater (median slope 1.7° in a 6 km CTX DEM window). Which Antofagasta sector would you pick?
quiz.sourceNote: Real data: Jezero CTX DEM (NASA MRO, USGS) vs. Copernicus GLO-30, at 30 m

options.pajonales: B) Salar de Pajonales cell (H3 83b221…, 4,200–5,270 m)

feedback.pajonales: Not this time: it is high-Andes terrain with much steeper slopes (median 7.9° vs. 1.7°; W₁ = 6.9°). A good example of what does NOT match Jezero.
feedback.yungay: Yungay is famous for its hyper-aridity, but its slopes are further from Jezero (W₁ = 3.3°) because it has steep hillsides. The classic analog is not always the best for every test.
feedback.pampa: Good pick! Its slope distribution differs from Jezero's by W₁ = 0.54° (95% CI: 0.40°–0.65°), and the result holds at 60 and 90 m. It is a candidate for field study, not a certified site: Mars gravity, pressure and radiation cannot be reproduced on Earth.

araucana.title: Antofagasta Territorial Impact & Caja La Araucana Strategic Alignment
araucana.antofagastaLabSubtitle: Click a regional node to load its 30 m terrain comparison (Jezero CTX DEM vs. Copernicus GLO-30) and its mission diagnostics:

nodes.pajonalesRole: Negative case: high-Andes cell (4,200–5,270 m) with much steeper slopes than Jezero (W₁ = 6.9° at 30 m).
nodes.cordilleraRole: Nearly flat (median slope 0.2°): smoother than the Jezero floor (W₁ = 1.7°, KS = 0.82).

home.tagline: Earth · Moon · Mars, compared with open NASA data
home.question: What matches? By how much? And what doesn't?
home.dataNote: Real example: an under-studied area of Antofagasta matches Jezero crater's slopes more closely than the classic Yungay analog (W₁ = 0.54° vs. 3.32°, at 30 m). We pre-select places to study; we do not certify them.
home.credits: Data: NASA, ESA and partner agencies. Ckepi is not affiliated with or endorsed by NASA.

problem.title: To reach the Moon and Mars, we test on Earth first
problem.body: Missions rehearse their equipment at places on Earth that resemble the Moon or Mars. But many are chosen by how they look, and other places that could help remain unstudied.

whatItDoes.title: CKEPI compares dimension by dimension
whatItDoes.body: Using open data from NASA and partner agencies, we compare terrain, climate and radiation on Earth, the Moon and Mars. For each place we show what matches, by how much, and what does not.

finding.title: A finding in Antofagasta
finding.body: At the same 30-metre scale, an under-studied area of the region (H3 cell 83b224) matches the slopes of Mars's Jezero crater more closely than the classic Yungay analog: a difference of 0.54° versus 3.32°.
finding.source: Data: Jezero CTX elevation model (NASA MRO, USGS) and Copernicus GLO-30 (ESA). Wasserstein-1 distance of slopes, 95% CI 0.40°–0.65°.

limits.title: What Earth cannot imitate
limits.body: On Mars, gravity is 0.38 times Earth's, the air is about 160 times thinner and radiation is much higher. No desert reproduces that. That is why CKEPI pre-selects places for field study; it does not certify them.

quiz.title: STEAM Mini-Challenge: Test Your Space Intuition
quiz.description: Use the simulators above to verify each answer experimentally.

q1.question: What happens to the mass (kg) and weight (N) of the Perseverance rover (1025 kg) on Mars?
q1.optA: Both its mass and weight drop to 38%
q1.optB: Its mass stays 1025 kg, while its weight in Newtons drops to 38%
q1.optC: Its weight in Newtons stays the same because of its metal wheels
q1.explanation: Correct! Mass is an intrinsic property (1025 kg anywhere), whereas weight depends on local gravity (W = m · g).

q2.question: In a vacuum (no atmosphere), which launch angle gives the maximum horizontal range on any planet?
q2.optA: It depends on the planet's gravity
q2.optB: 75° on the Moon and 30° on Earth
q2.explanation: Without atmospheric drag, sin(2θ) peaks at θ = 45° regardless of the value of g.

q3.question: Compared to Earth, a shallow-water wave in a 5 m deep lunar basin travels...
q3.optA: Slower, because c = √(g · h) and lunar gravity is weaker
q3.optB: Faster, because water weighs less on the Moon
q3.optC: At the exact same speed on both worlds
q3.explanation: Gravity is the restoring force for surface waves: weaker gravity means slower wave propagation (2.85 m/s on the Moon vs. 7.00 m/s on Earth).

atmosphere.title: Air Chemical Composition & Respiratory Habitability (Earth · Mars · Moon)
atmosphere.description: Compare the chemical compounds of each world and how Earth’s gas balance is optimal for human physiology versus life-support (ECLSS / ISRU) challenges on Mars and the Moon.

earth.summary: Ideal balance: 21% O₂ for cellular respiration and 78% N₂ as an inert buffer gas that keeps lung alveoli open and suppresses fire hazards.

mars.summary: Ultra-thin atmosphere with 95.3% CO₂ (lethal hypercapnia) and virtually zero O₂. However, atmospheric CO₂ enables in-situ O₂ production via NASA MOXIE.

moon.summary: No breathable gaseous atmosphere, but ~43% of lunar regolith mass is oxygen bound in metal oxides, plus water ice in polar craters.

roles.n2Earth: Nitrogen: Inert buffer gas maintaining alveolar pressure without toxicity and driving the nitrogen cycle.
roles.o2Earth: Oxygen: Essential electron acceptor for aerobic cellular respiration (ATP).
roles.co2Earth: Carbon dioxide: Triggers breathing reflex at trace levels and maintains mild greenhouse warmth.
roles.co2Mars: Carbon dioxide: Causes immediate hypercapnia in humans, but serves as feedstock for MOXIE O₂ generation.
roles.n2Mars: Nitrogen: Present at 2.7%; must be concentrated to provide habitat buffer gas.
roles.o2CoMars: Trace O₂ (0.13%) and toxic carbon monoxide (CO, 0.08%).
roles.regolithO2: Mineral-bound oxygen in regolith: Extractable by heating Si, Fe, and Ti oxides (>900 °C).
roles.polarIce: Water ice in permanently shadowed polar craters (Shackleton): Ideal for electrolysis.
roles.exosphere: Vestigial exosphere: Sparse atoms that cannot support breathing or sound.

pillars.o2Desc: Below 100 mbar causes cerebral hypoxia and unconsciousness; above 500 mbar causes pulmonary oxygen toxicity and extreme fire risk.
pillars.n2Title: 2. Why Nitrogen Buffer Gas (78% N₂) Is Essential
pillars.n2Desc: Breathing pure oxygen collapses lung alveoli (absorption atelectasis) and turns sparks into infernos. N₂ safely dilutes O₂ and provides total pressure.
pillars.co2Title: 3. Critical CO₂ (< 5 mbar) & Pressure (> 63 mbar) Limits
pillars.co2Desc: Even with enough O₂, >1%–2% CO₂ prevents blood from offloading carbon dioxide. On Mars, CO₂ makes up 95.3% of the gas mix.
